episode_title: Time Management for Construction Leaders: Stop Fighting Fires

real_qa.q: How does the Eisenhower Matrix help construction leaders stop firefighting and focus on fire prevention?
real_qa.r: The Eisenhower Matrix sorts tasks into four boxes: Box One contains long-range priorities that are important but not urgent (fire prevention work like strategic planning and client meetings); Box Two contains critical activities that are both important and urgent (fires you must handle immediately); Box Three contains interruptions that are urgent but not important to you; and Box Four contains distractions. Fire prevention happens in Box One, and it is the only way to shrink or prevent the fires that occur in Boxes Two and Three. Most construction company owners spend their week in Boxes Two and Three with a hose in their hands, but owners should spend most of their time in Box One doing activities that prevent fires.
real_qa.requete: Eisenhower Matrix construction leaders time management

real_qa.q: What are the three critical areas where fires start in construction companies and how should owners block time for each?
real_qa.r: Fires in construction companies start in three places: sales, operations, and people. For sales prevention, owners should create a weekly block and make a list of their top 10 clients and prospects, then schedule breakfast, lunch, coffee, or phone calls with them. For operations, owners should block time to find where schedules slip, where the company is unsafe, and where quality falls short. For people, owners must get crystal clear on the people they want technically and culturally, define what excellence looks like in hiring, and hold people accountable for executing their roles. If owners skip this work, fires keep popping up and the company stays stressed out with projects running late and poor quality.
real_qa.requete: three areas fires start construction company owner time blocks

real_qa.q: How many hours per year can construction leaders lose to workplace interruptions and what causes attention residue?
real_qa.r: A project manager named Daniel tracked his time for one week and found he was spending three hours a day on interruptions from other people. Multiplying three hours a day across 220 working days equals 660 hours per year—more than 16 forty-hour work weeks. Sophie Leroy, who studies how people focus at work, found that when you switch from one task to another, part of your mind stays stuck on the last task, which she calls attention residue. Every interruption costs you not only the time it takes but also the focus you do not get back right away.
real_qa.requete: interruptions construction leaders 660 hours year attention residue

real_qa.q: What is time blocking and what are the three main types of blocks that do most of the work?
real_qa.r: Time blocking means giving every hour a job before the week starts so your inbox and interruptions do not control your calendar. The three blocks that do most of the work are: a focus block, which is 90 minutes on a Box One priority with the door closed, alerts off, and your phone on the other side of the room; office hours, which are set two times a day when your people know they can find you and bring their issues to you; and a buffer of 60 minutes a day with nothing in it because something always goes sideways on a job site. A time block only works if you keep it, name it clearly (like 'Strategic plan' or 'top 10 client lunch'), communicate it to your people, and hold yourself accountable to it.
real_qa.requete: time blocking construction leaders focus block office hours

real_qa.q: How long does it take to regain focus after an interruption according to research?
real_qa.r: Gloria Mark at UC Irvine in California found that it takes about 23 minutes to get back to the work you were pulled off of when you experience an interruption. This research demonstrates why protecting time blocks and minimizing interruptions is critical for construction leaders' productivity.
real_qa.requete: Gloria Mark UC Irvine 23 minutes interruption focus recovery
